claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase bcc at high temperature.
The initial alloy has a random atomic distribution at high temperature.
Controlled annealing or rapid quenching can induce percolating SRO clusters while preserving the single-phase bcc structure.
An adequate potential-energy surface must capture multi-body interactions to reproduce SRO evolution.
Percolating chemically ordered clusters act as a distinct phonon-transport channel rather than solely as isolated scattering centers.
Isolated SRO defects scatter phonons and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolation of SRO clusters creates a connected sub-lattice with vibrational properties distinct from those of the disordered matrix.
An SRO network with lower phonon-scattering rates or higher group velocities than the disordered matrix would facilitate percolative phonon transport.
Percolative transport can override the scattering-dominated behavior predicted by serial/parallel mixing models.
Thermal conductivity will undergo a sharp, non-linear change at a critical SRO cluster size or density corresponding to a percolation threshold.
The conductivity change may be a sudden increase or a plateau relative to linear mixing behavior.
Standard serial/parallel mixing models and simple point-defect scattering theories predict a monotonic reduction in thermal conductivity as SRO concentration increases.
The proposed percolative effect is restricted to single-phase bcc systems in which SRO clusters physically percolate.
The proposed effect does not apply when SRO remains isolated or when phase separation occurs.
Machine-learning potentials can be constructed to capture SRO evolution and correlate SRO topology with thermal conductivity.
